paragraphs.heading: Water on the move
paragraphs.text: Transpiration is the movement of water through a plant and its evaporation from parts above ground, such as leaves, stems and flowers. The name comes from Latin and means, roughly, the act of breathing across. It is a passive process, so the plant spends no energy on it. Along the way it cools the plant, changes the osmotic pressure of cells and lets mineral nutrients travel in mass flow.

paragraphs.heading: Where the water goes
paragraphs.text: Plants need water, yet only a small share of what their roots take up is used for growth and metabolism. Between 97 and 99.5 percent leaves again through transpiration and guttation. Over a growing season a single leaf gives off many times its own weight in water. An acre of corn releases about 11,000 to 15,000 liters a day, and a large oak can transpire 150,000 liters a year. Crops typically lose 200 to 1000 kg of water for every kilogram of dry matter they build.

paragraphs.heading: The pull from the leaves
paragraphs.text: Roots absorb water and dissolved minerals by osmosis, and the water rises through the xylem to the leaves and out through small pores called stomata. The cohesion-tension theory explains how leaves do the pulling. Water molecules stick to each other, so when one evaporates from a leaf it tugs on its neighbour, keeping a continuous stream. When the outside air has a lower water potential than the air space in a stoma, vapour moves out, and liquid water evaporates from the cell walls inside the leaf. The tension this creates passes through the leaf cells to the xylem, drawing water up from the roots. Capillary action helps a little, but differences in water potential do most of the work.

paragraphs.heading: Turning the rate up or down
paragraphs.text: Each stoma is bordered by guard cells that open and close it, and plants set their transpiration rate by changing the size of these openings. The air around the leaf matters too: humidity, temperature, wind and sunlight all change how fast water leaves. Soil temperature and moisture can affect stomatal opening, and a plant's size and the water its roots absorb also count. When roots cannot keep up with the loss, the plant closes its stomata. That saves water but slows nutrient uptake and cuts the carbon dioxide it takes in, holding back photosynthesis and growth.

paragraphs.heading: Desert answers
paragraphs.text: Desert plants have features that hold water in, such as thick cuticles, smaller leaf areas, sunken stomata and hairs. Many cacti carry out photosynthesis in fleshy stems instead of leaves, which keeps the surface area of the shoot very low. Many desert plants also use crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, keeping their stomata shut by day and opening them at night, when transpiration is lower.

paragraphs.heading: When the supply breaks
paragraphs.text: To keep the pressure gradient it needs, a plant must keep drawing in water through its roots fast enough to replace what it transpires. If it cannot, an event called cavitation occurs. The xylem starts filling with water vapour instead of liquid water, and the vapour gathers into blockages. Those blockages stop the plant from moving water through its vascular system.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring it
paragraphs.text: Scientists measure transpiration with several tools, among them potometers, lysimeters, porometers and thermometric sap flow sensors. Isotope measurements show that transpiration is the bigger part of evapotranspiration.
